# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: memory
function.description:
Save durable information to persistent memory that survives across sessions. Memory is injected into future turns, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.

WHEN TO SAVE (do this proactively, don't wait to be asked):
- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup
- You identify a stable fact that will be useful again in future sessions

PRIORITY: User preferences and corrections > environment facts > procedural knowledge. The most valuable memory prevents the user from having to repeat themselves.

Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts.
If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

TWO TARGETS:
- 'user': who the user is -- name, role, preferences, communication style, pet peeves
- 'memory': your notes -- environment facts, project conventions, tool quirks, lessons learned

ACTIONS: add (new entry), replace (update existing -- old_text identifies it), remove (delete -- old_text identifies it).

SKIP: trivial/obvious info, things easily re-discovered, raw data dumps, and temporary task state.

target.description: Which memory store: 'memory' for personal notes, 'user' for user profile.

content.description: The entry content. Required for 'add' and 'replace'.

old_text.description: Short unique substring identifying the entry to replace or remove.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

On delete, pass `absorbed_into=<umbrella>` when you're merging this skill's content into another one, or `absorbed_into=""` when you're pruning it with no forwarding target. This lets the curator tell consolidation from pruning without guessing, so downstream consumers (cron jobs that reference the old skill name, etc.) get updated correctly. The target you name in `absorbed_into` must already exist — create/patch the umbrella first, then delete.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

Pinned skills are protected from deletion only — skill_manage(action='delete') will refuse with a message pointing the user to `hermes curator unpin <name>`. Patches and edits go through on pinned skills so you can still improve them as pitfalls come up; pin only guards against irrecoverable loss.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

category.description: Optional category/domain for organizing the skill (e.g., 'devops', 'data-science', 'mlops'). Creates a subdirectory grouping. Only used with 'create'.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

file_content.description: Content for the file. Required for 'write_file'.

absorbed_into.description: For 'delete' only — declares intent so the curator can tell consolidation from pruning without guessing. Pass the umbrella skill name when this skill's content was merged into another (the target must already exist). Pass an empty string when the skill is truly stale and being pruned with no forwarding target. Omitting the arg on delete is supported for backward compatibility but downstream tooling (e.g. cron-job skill reference rewriting) will have to guess at intent.

# Book Marketing Launch Campaign

Low/no-cost book marketing strategy and deployment system for self-published Kindle books.

## Per-Book Marketing Strategy

### For Business/How-To Books (e.g., "AI That Works for Small Business")

**Core Strategy:** LinkedIn authority content + free Kindle promotion + small-business community outreach.

**Don't advertise the book first.** Teach one useful lesson per day:
- Share one small-business problem
- Present one AI workflow that solves it  
- Give one example prompt
- Show one useful result
- Softly point readers to the Kindle book

**Best Channels (ranked):**
1. **A** — LinkedIn posts and comments
2. **A-** — Local business Facebook groups
3. **A-** — Email to existing contacts
4. **B+** — KDP Select free promotion
5. **B** — Podcasts and local business associations
6. **B-** — Amazon ads at $3-$5/day

**Best Message Hook:** *"Here are 25 ways a small business can save 5 hours a week with AI."*

**Target Audience:** Small business owners, entrepreneurs, solopreneurs, operations managers.

### For Memoir/History/Psychology Books (e.g., "Tomorrow Is Still Open")

**Core Strategy:** Story excerpts + book-club positioning + Substack/LinkedIn/Facebook community distribution.

**Main Hook:** *"One life. Seventy years of history. Seventy years of possible future. What changed? What did not? What do humans keep repeating?"*

**Best Campaign:** Run a "14 Stories Across 140 Years" campaign (14-day).

**Best Channels (ranked):**
1. **A** — Substack (best for serialized memoir)
2. **A** — Book clubs (discussion-rich content)
3. **A-** — Facebook groups (nostalgia, history, futurism)
4. **B+** — LinkedIn (thought-leadership angles)
5. **B** — Goodreads
6. **B-** — Amazon free/discount promotion

**Best Positioning:** *"A personal journey through memory, history, psychology, and the future."*

**Best Lead Magnet:** *"70 Years Back / 70 Years Forward: Book Club Questions"* — free download.

## Deployment System

Create a `book-launch-system/` folder with this structure:

```
book-launch-system/
├── book-info.md           ← title, subtitle, author, Amazon link, description, author bio, 3 excerpts
├── audience-map.md        ← who buys this book, where they hang out, what they care about
├── content-pillars.md     ← 5-7 content themes for posts
├── substack/              ← serialized excerpt series
├── book-clubs/            ← discussion guide, flyer, outreach
├── facebook-groups/       ← group-specific post drafts
└── tracking/              ← launch metrics
```

### Substack Deployment

Create a 7-part series (title varies per book):

For memoir books: **"70 Years Back / 70 Years Forward"**

Suggested issues:
1. The Question That Started the Book
2. What Memory Keeps and History Forgets
3. The Psychology of Fear Across Generations
4. Technology Changes. Human Nature Repeats.
5. What the Last 70 Years Taught Me
6. What the Next 70 Years Might Ask of Us
7. A Letter to Readers in the Future

Each issue should be 800-1500 words — excerpt from the book with original framing.

### Book-Club Deployment

Create these files:
- `discussion-guide.md` — 10-15 questions, grouped by theme
- `one-page-book-club-flyer.md` — formatted summary for distribution
- `outreach-list.csv` — Book club names, contact info, genre focus
- `outreach-email-templates.md` — Cold email + follow-up templates
- `follow-up-log.csv` — Track who was contacted and responses

The **discussion guide** should be offered as a free lead magnet on Substack and social media.

### Facebook Groups Deployment

- Create group-specific drafts (one per target group type)
- Manually post only after reading group rules
- Use value-first discussion questions, not direct links
- Include versions WITH and WITHOUT links
- Groups to target:
  - Small business owners (for business books)
  - History enthusiasts (for memoir)
  - Psychology/memory (for memoir)
  - Nostalgia/70s/80s (for memoir with generational content)
  - Futurism/sci-fi (for memoir covering future speculation)

## 30-Day Launch Calendar

### Week 1 — Setup & Drafting
- [ ] Set up Substack profile/publication
- [ ] Draft all 7 Substack issues
- [ ] Create book-club kit (discussion guide, flyer, email templates)
- [ ] Build outreach list (20+ book clubs)
- [ ] Draft 10 Facebook group posts
- [ ] Create book-launch-system/ folder with all files

### Week 2 — Launch First Wave
- [ ] Publish Substack Issue 1
- [ ] Manually post 2 Facebook discussion posts
- [ ] Contact 5 libraries/book clubs via email
- [ ] Ask 5 early readers for honest reviews
- [ ] Post first LinkedIn educational content (business book) or story excerpt (memoir)

### Week 3 — Expand
- [ ] Publish Substack Issue 2
- [ ] Manually post 2 more Facebook discussion posts
- [ ] Contact 5 more groups/clubs
- [ ] Share the discussion guide publicly (free download)
- [ ] Post second LinkedIn/Facebook round

### Week 4 — Sustain & Measure
- [ ] Publish Substack Issue 3
- [ ] Post a launch reflection on all channels
- [ ] Follow up with all contacted book clubs
- [ ] Review metrics — repeat what worked
- [ ] Plan for Issues 4-7 based on engagement

## Safety Rules (Must Follow)

- **Never auto-post into Facebook Groups** — must be manual, human-approved
- **Never auto-message followers at scale** — use Message Ads or opt-in CRM/email instead
- **Never scrape people, groups, member lists, or private posts**
- **Never publish anything without user approval**
- **Hermes should automate: drafting, scheduling files, reminders, tracking, approved platform actions**
- **Hermes should NOT auto-post or spam communities**

## Agent Work Order Template

When user asks to deploy a book launch:

> "Create the full book-launch-system folder. Use the book concept below:
> - Book title: [title]
> - Amazon link: [link]
> - Description: [description]
> - Author bio: [bio]
> - 3 favorite excerpts: [excerpts]
> 
> Create all files in book-launch-system/. Show me:
> 1. The 30-day calendar
> 2. First Substack issue draft
> 3. First 3 Facebook group posts
> 
> Wait for my approval before publishing or scheduling anything."

## Related Skills & Pipeline

**Related Skills:**
- `book-deliverable-kdp` — Build KDP packages (precedes marketing)
- `book-identity-rebranding` — Rename books before marketing

**Pipeline Integration:** References this skill as the marketing layer in the publishing workflow.

{"content": "    31|Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.
    32|
    33|The key made contact.
    34|
    35|Electricity is invisible. They see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost they've domesticated. In that moment, Bob met that ghost directly. The shock surged through his body with the indifferent authority of physics acting on matter. His muscles clenched. His arm locked. The force threw him backward across the kitchen. Bob landed in a heap against the far wall.
    36|
    37|Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped thing. His hand—*oh, his hand*—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours. Bob sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, his body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.
    38|
    39|Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—his mother's eyes wide, his father's jaw set. They found him crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between him and the outlet, the story written clearly without a single word spoken.
    40|
    41|The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. Bob was told what Bob already knew, what his body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.
    42|
    43|And yet.
    44|
    45|Here is the part that still surprises him, seventy years later. Despite the terror. Despite the scolding. Despite the tingle that lingered in his hand for hours afterward—Bob felt exhilaration. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, Bob had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. Bob had asked a question of the universe—*what will happen?*—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.
    46|
    47|This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment a child realizes the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.
    48|
    49|### What Bob Remember vs. What Bob Was Told
    50|
    51|But here they must pause, because Bob cannot be entirely certain this memory belongs to him. The mind is a trickster, a master forger of its own past. Cognitive science has proven this beyond doubt: every time they recall a memory, they reconstruct it. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what happened and what they believe happened becomes porous, eventually indistinguishable.
    52|
    53|His mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as Bob grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—his fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of his body hitting the wall, the expression on his father's face. Did Bob remembered these things? Or did Bob remembered *her* remembering them?
    54|
    55|The memory Bob carry feels real. Bob can feel the cool metal of the key. Bob can taste the ozone in the air afterward. But feeling real and *being* real are different things. A false memory can be as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience. Bob have studied the neuroscience since then. Bob know about synaptic plasticity, about long-term potentiation. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. Bob still cannot say with certainty whether Bob remembered the shock itself or only remember his mother telling him about it.
    56|
    57|Perhaps that ambiguity is itself the lesson.
    58|
    59|### The Spark That Lit a Life
    60|
    61|What is *not* ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of his life. Whether Bob actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed Bob had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in him—a fascination with electricity that evolved into a passion for science and technology spanning seven decades.
    62|
    63|In the months and years that followed, Bob devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. Bob conducted home experiments—some dangerous, all illuminating. Bob built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles governing the invisible force that had once thrown him across a kitchen. His parents, recognizing that his curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured his endeavors. They bought him books. They tolerated the mess. They learned to check the fuse box after Bob had been "working" in the basement.
    64|
    65|That passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.
    66|
    67|The gift of that moment was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. It taught him that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands they touch the very things they're warned against. It taught him that the most formative moments of their lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether Bob actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that Bob *believe* Bob did—that this belief shaped his curiosity, his career, his very identity.
    68|
    69|The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming.
    70|
    71|That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement. Because something far more distant than a kitchen outlet was about to begin beeping its way across the night sky, and the child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was about to discover that the universe held reaches extending far beyond anything he could yet imagine.
    72|
    73|Chapter Two: The Echoes of Sputnik and a Family Legacy
    74|
    75|The beep came from everywhere and nowhere at once in 1957. Five years old, Bob sat cross-legged on the worn linoleum floor of his grandparents' living room, eyes fixed on the radio console that dominated the corner like a mahogany cathedral. The voice on the broadcast spoke words Bob couldn't fully comprehend—something about Russians, a silver sphere now circling the Earth, a new age dawning while America slept. Beep. Beep. Beep. That sound—mechanical, relentless, somehow both cold and alive—lodged in his bones and stayed there for seven decades and counting.
    76|
    77|Bob didn't understand what Bob was witnessing. How could Bob? Bob was a child of the Midwest, raised in a world where televisions were still novelties and telephones came with party lines. The Space Age might as well have been the Stone Age for all the context his five-year-old mind could offer. But something about that beeping signal registered anyway, deep in his subconscious—a recognition that the world had shifted on its axis, that the comfortable boundaries of his young life had suddenly expanded to include not just his street and his town, but the infinite black canvas above.
    78|
    79|---
    80|
    81|If Sputnik represented humanity reaching upward, his family roots ran deep in the opposite direction—into iron rails and coal smoke and the rhythmic chug of locomotive engines. His grandfather was a locomotive engineer back when that title meant something almost sacred. In the early twentieth century, engineers weren't mere operators; they were craftsmen, masters of machines built by hand in foundries where every piston and valve bore the fingerprints of its maker. A photograph survives from that era: him perched atop an enormous black locomotive, his small hand gripping the cast-iron railing, his grandfather beside him with a wave that seemed to say, *This is yours, boy. This tradition of building, of making the immovable move—this is your inheritance.* Bob didn't remember the photograph being taken. Bob only remember the photograph itself, studied so many times its edges softened and its colors faded into sepia.
    82|
    83|His great-grandfather, Robert Charters, carried the storytelling tradition further. When Bob was eight, the old man—already ravaged by consumption, eating baby food from glass jars that seemed to mock his diminished state—would summon him with a gesture learned in another century. "Remember, lad," he would rasp, his voice carrying the weight of Scottish highlands, Canadian wilderness, and the Michigan lumber camps where their family had finally put down roots. "We Mills have the blood of builders and engineers."
    84|
    85|Then came the stories that burned brightest. Knights Templar, he claimed—medieval warrior-monks who fought bloody Crusades, then transformed themselves into Europe's master builders, constructing the soaring Gothic cathedrals that still inspire awe. From protectors of pilgrims to moneylenders, from stone masons to bankers—the trajectory seemed improbable and somehow fitting for a family that would eventually produce locomotive engineers and, eventually, him.
    86|
    87|Years later, genealogical research found no documentary evidence of Templar connections. They were stories, embroidered and enhanced through generations of retelling until they achieved the density of myth. But sitting at that old man's bedside, watching his thin fingers gesture through the air as he described cathedrals rising from nothing, Bob didn't need proof. Whether his veins carried Templar blood was irrelevant. What mattered was that Bob believed himself part of a lineage of builders, of problem-solvers, of men who looked at raw materials and saw possibility. That belief shaped everything that followed. It still does.
    88|
    89|---
    90|
    91|To understand his father, you have to understand the crucible that forged him. Bob Sr. grew up an only child in a world bounded by an elementary school and a family home. When World War II erupted, it pulled him into something vast and terrifying. At seventeen, he enlisted in the Navy and found himself responsible for the electrical systems of a scow—a flat-bottomed workhorse that served the fleet in dangerous, unsung ways. He lived in cramped quarters with engine noise so constant it became a form of silence, snatched sleep in thirty-minute intervals between watches. He graduated to an aircraft carrier, where the stakes grew heavier. As a master electrician, he held lives in his hands every time he traced a circuit or repaired a generator. One mistake could mean planes unable to launch, pumps unable to fight fires, communications severed at the moment of maximum danger.
    92|
    93|He returned from the Pacific War changed, carrying things no seventeen-year-old should bear. He married his mother in a clandestine elopement—Catholic and Protestant, their families wouldn't bless the union, the old hatred running deep enough to cut. They moved into his parents' partially finished, unheated summer cottage, two young people trying to build a life in a structure meant for vacation weekends. Then came the recall.
    94|
    95|When North Korean forces poured across the 38th parallel in 1950, his father's decision to stay in the Naval Reserves—made for sensible peacetime reasons—became a doorway back into war. He served on an aircraft carrier through the Korean conflict, returning to Michigan only after the armistice of 1953. By then, his mother was pregnant with their first child, a boy they named Robert, after the generations of Roberts before him. The GI Bill bought what would otherwise have been impossible: a small home with a low-cost mortgage, a foothold in the American middle class for a working-class sailor with an elementary school education. Bob was born in the fall of 1952. A baby brother followed. The family was complete, or so it seemed.
    96|
    97|---
    98|
    99|His earliest coherent memories of his father are of a man in perpetual vigilance, as if still standing watch on a carrier deck. Saturdays in the Mills household were not days of rest. They were days of chores, inspections, tasks assigned with military precision and expected to military standards. He treated them not as children but as raw recruits who needed breaking down and rebuilding into capable men. For him, the firstborn, the emotional support he intended often got lost in translation, drowned out by the sheer volume of his voice. That voice. It wasn't that he was angry—not really—but he had learned to project authority across engine rooms and flight decks, to make himself heard over the scream of jets and the roar of machinery. When he brought that voice home, he thought he was preparing them for a world he knew to be unforgiving. What he never understood was that a child is not a sailor, and a living room is not a ship. Bob see that now. Bob didn't then. Bob just knew that sound meant Bob would done something wrong, or was about to.
   100|
   101|His younger brother resisted passively. He would rock nervously, wait out the storm. But Bob took a different path. Bob learned to comply, to anticipate, to internalize the expectations until they became his own. Bob cleaned his room. Bob completed his chores without complaint. Bob tried, in essence, to become the model sailor his father wanted, never quite reaching the adult standards Bob would set for himself.
   102|
   103|There was tenderness in him, too, though it came sideways. He was a craftsman of extraordinary versatility—electrician by trade, but also plumber, carpenter, model builder. He found his peace in the garage, surrounded by the scent of sawdust and glue, constructing U-control and radio-controlled aircraft from balsa wood and tissue paper. These weren't toys; they were engineering challenges demanding the same precision as their full-sized counterparts. That garage became his summer classroom. He taught him to read blueprints, to calculate weight distributions, to understand the aerodynamic principles that kept fragile structures aloft. Other neighborhood boys joined them, drawn by the spectacle of flight and the quiet charisma of a man who could make the impossible seem achievable. He never turned a boy away. The garage became a sanctuary for a whole generation of young people seeking the approval of a father figure who demanded excellence and returned the satisfaction of creation. Years later, Bob recognized the pattern: his harshness and his generosity, his demanding nature and his dedication—all facets of a man trying to love his sons in the only language he knew. By the time his third brother arrived, his father had softened considerably. Experience taught him that children weren't sailors, that love didn't require drill sergeant volume. But for him, the firstborn, the die was already cast.
   104|
   105|---
   106|
   107|If the garage represented his father at his best, the dinner table was something more complicated. His parents carried the weight of their generation—the legacy of Depression-era scarcity and wartime rationing that had programmed their bodies to treat every meal as potentially the last. Providing food was love. Making children eat that food was responsibility. And ensuring nothing was wasted—*clean your plate*—was moral duty inherited from ancestors who knew genuine hunger.
   108|
   109|The problem was that his father had no conception of child-sized portions. He heaped their plates with adult quantities of meat and potatoes and vegetables. And when he said “clean your plate,” he meant it. They did not leave the table until every scrap was consumed.
   110|
   111|His younger brother rebelled. He would sit for hours, stubbornly refusing to finish, willing to endure punishment rather than force down food his body couldn’t accommodate. But Bob was different. Bob learned to eat. Bob cleaned his plate because that was what was expected, what was demanded, what made him worthy of his father’s approval. Bob ate past the point of fullness, past the point of comfort, past the point where his body sent clear signals of satiety. Slowly, inevitably, Bob lost track of what “full” even felt like.
   112|
   113|His parents never called him fat. They used the euphemism “husky,” as if the word itself could reshape reality. But the reality was that Bob grew up overweight—the product of forced consumption, of food tangled up with approval and safety and the avoidance of conflict. His father didn’t understand any of this. He was feeding his sons, ensuring they grew up strong, preparing them for a demanding world. That he might be programming his firstborn for a lifetime struggle with weight and health and self-image never occurred to him. He was overweight himself, locked in his own battles with the scale, unable to recognize the patterns he was passing down.
   114|
   115|---
   116|
   117|### The Neuroscience of Addiction
   118|
   119|Neuroscience would later give Bob a language for what had happened to him. The brain’s reward circuits—the same pathways that evolved to reinforce survival behaviors like eating—had been hijacked by the very act of forced overconsumption. Each time Bob cleaned his plate past the point of fullness, his brain encoded a pattern: compliance equals safety equals reward. The dopamine system, designed to motivate seeking food in times of scarcity, learned instead to drive consumption in times of plenty.
   120|
   121|Bob’s father and mother were both overweight. They viewed providing food and making children eat it as part of their parenting role, a duty passed down from generations who had known genuine hunger. At dinner time Bob’s father would dish out an adult portion and require his son to eat it all. In his mind, making a child clean his plate was good parenting. His younger brother resisted, but Bob learned to eat it all, and in the process lost his sense of being full.
   122|
   123|The combination of bad habits, genetics, stress, and an impulsive personality helped Bob grow up overweight. His parents would never say he was fat—they would only describe Bob as “husky.” The word was a shield, a way of avoiding the truth that they had, through love and concern, set their son on a path toward a lifelong struggle.
   124|
   125|---
   126|
   127|### The Adult Battle
   128|
   129|When Bob left home for college, freed from his father’s dinner table, he shed the pounds. The discipline he had learned in the garage—focus, persistence, attention to detail—served him well. He exercised, controlled his portions, found a weight that felt sustainable. For a few years, Bob was fit. Then came career, marriage, children, the inevitable stresses of supporting a family in a high-pressure world. Bob’s relationship with food morphed into a maze of emotions. It was no longer just about eating; it became a psychological crutch.
   130|
   131|The weight returned, and with it high blood pressure, diabetes, the slow accumulation of damage that excess weight inflicts. Unbeknownst to him, the food addiction that had started in childhood had deepened into something medical, something that neuroscientific research now links to the same memory circuits that record formative experiences. These circuits, once hijacked by addictive behaviors, become difficult to break free from.
   132|
   133|After his first wife died, the pattern accelerated. Bob’s life became a series of rendezvous with sugary, fatty, and salty temptations. He would often find himself in empty conference rooms at work, scavenging for stale donuts left over from morning meetings. The room would become a sanctuary, a place where he could momentarily escape the haunting void left by Nancy’s passing. The sugar and fat provided momentary relief from grief—a chemical holiday from the weight of loss.
   134|
   135|His body betrayed him, accumulating weight, bringing high blood pressure and diabetes deeper into his life. But it was not just the physical toll. Emotionally, he felt like a ship caught in a storm, tossed around by waves of anxiety and depression. The memory of his father’s voice—*Clean your plate or you will not leave the table*—echoed in his mind not as words but as something deeper, a pattern encoded in his nervous system, every time Bob reached for comfort.
   136|
   137|---
   138|
   139|### The Road Back
   140|
   141|Yet the human spirit is resilient. Bob knew he was spiraling, and he also knew he had the power to pull himself back. The same determination that had carried him through engineering problems and career challenges now had to be turned inward. Through weight loss therapy and professional guidance, Bob discovered that his addiction was a complex web woven from genetic predispositions, environmental triggers, and deeply ingrained psychological patterns. He learned that memory plays a crucial role in eating disorders—it is not just about eating less, but about remembering the emotional states that food has been trained to alter.
   142|
   143|With newfound knowledge and professional help, Bob embarked on a years-long journey to reclaim his life, losing over two hundred pounds through exercise and strict weight management. The discipline that had served him in the garage and the boardroom now served him in the gym and at the dinner table. Years later, he gained back forty pounds, then lost them again. The fight is ongoing. Bob knows that food addiction, like any addiction, is something he will need to manage for the rest of his life.
   144|
   145|Understanding was the first step toward healing. Bob had traced a direct line from that childhood dinner table to his adult struggles, and in doing so had found the path back to himself. His father had been a good man who did not understand the impact of his parenting. Bob’s father himself was overweight and never intended harm. Studies show that early life experiences and memories significantly influence eating behaviors and disorders later in life. Bob had become living proof of that research—and also proof that the patterns can be broken.
   146|
   147|---
   148|That is how memory shapes them. Not as a passive record but as an active participant in the ongoing construction of who they are. The beep of Sputnik became wonder. The locomotive became heritage. The garage became skill. Even the dinner table, with all its weight, became understanding—of his father, of himself, of the complicated ways love and damage can intertwine. Bob stand now at the intersection of all these memories, looking back with the clarity age provides and forward with the hope that has sustained him through every challenge. The echoes of 1957 still sound in his mind, but time and reflection have transformed them into something richer than recollection. They have become wisdom.
   149|
   150|### The Echoes
   151|
   152|The beep of Sputnik. The chug of his grandfather's locomotive. The roar of his father's voice. The clink of fork against plate in a silent kitchen where a child learned to override his own body's wisdom. These memories are not separate strands but a single thread, woven through the fabric of Bob's identity. They represent the intersection of personal history and world history, of individual psychology and generational trauma. The Space Age gave him his dreams; his family gave him the tools to pursue them; and the difficult lessons of his childhood gave him both the drive to succeed and the vulnerabilities he would spend a lifetime learning to manage. Bob's father mellowed as he aged, his military bearing softening into something approaching tenderness he rarely showed and his eventual grandchildren has a hard time seeing. He would tell his son, in rare moments of vulnerability, that his mission had been to make Bob a better man than he himself was. In the end, he succeeded—though not in the ways he had planned. Bob became a different kind of father, a different kind of man, learning from his father's mistakes while honoring his intentions.
   153|
   154|When Bob had his own son, he found himself echoing his father's words, but without the yelling. The cycle had come full circle, modified by the wisdom that comes with generational distance. He had internalized the valuable lessons—the importance of discipline, of craftsmanship, of showing up and doing the work—while trying filtering out the damage. He made many mistakes and was far from perfect, but he did better than his father and hoped that his son would be a better father than himself.
   155|
   156|This is how memory shapes them: not as passive record but as active participant in the ongoing construction of self. The beep of Sputnik became wonder. The locomotive became heritage. The garage became skill. Even the dinner table, with all its trauma, became understanding—of his father, of himself, of the complex ways that love and damage can intertwine. Bob stands now at the intersection of all these memories, looking back with the clarity that age provides and forward with the hope that has sustained him through every challenge. The echoes of 1957 still sound in his mind, but they have been transformed by time and reflection into something richer than mere recollection. They have become wisdom.
   157|
   158|Chapter Three: Mr. Chips
   159|
   160|The summer Bob turned seven, his father came home with a dog.
   161|
   162|Bob remembered the screen door slapping shut, that loose spring never quite catching. And then a sound Bob would never heard in their house before. Clicking. Nails on linoleum. And the softest, most tentative whimper from anything alive.
   163|
   164|His name was Mr. Chips, and he was a mongrel—a fierce protector for their family, his father announced. But he was wrong about that. Chips wasn't a guard dog. He was his first real friend.
   165|
   166|He had a coat as black as midnight, the kind that swallowed light, with a single white tip at the end of his tail—like someone had dipped it in paint as an afterthought. His eyes were brown, warm and uncertain, the eyes of an animal who had already learned the world could be cruel. His father bought him from a shelter, and you could see it in the way he moved those first few days. Careful. Measuring every step. Waiting for the other shoe to drop.
   167|
   168|Bob remembered the first time Bob touched him. Bob was sitting cross-legged on the kitchen floor, and he walked over slowly, head low, that white-tipped tail giving one tentative wag. He sniffed his hand—his nose cold and wet against his knuckles—and then he let out this sigh. Not a whimper. Just a long, slow exhale, like he'd been holding his breath his whole life and finally let it go. He laid his head on his knee, and Bob felt the weight of it. The warmth of his skull through his jeans. From that moment, they were inseparable.
   169|
   170|For four years, Chips and Bob were a unit. He slept at the foot of his bed every night, a warm, breathing lump that rose and fell in the dark. In the mornings his face would be inches from mine, tail thumping against the mattress, waiting for him to wake up. His bark was sharp and sudden, a single explosive WOOF that startled him even when Bob knew it was coming. He smelled like dust and pine and something warm and animal Bob had never been able to name since.
   171|
   172|They played in the woods behind the house. Bob would throw sticks and he'd tear after them, crashing through ferns, that white-tipped tail disappearing into the green. He'd come back with leaves stuck to his fur and mud caked on his paws, tongue hanging out, looking at him like Bob was the best thing that had ever happened to him. And Bob thought maybe Bob was. He certainly was for him.
   173|
   174|Then one day he didn't come back.
   175|
   176|He'd run off into the woods, same as always. But the sun went down, and he wasn't at the door. His mother called and called into the dark. Nothing.
   177|
   178|They searched everywhere. His father, his mother, him—fanning out through the woods, calling his name until their voices went hoarse. His legs were scratched raw from branches. Bob remembered the silence between calls, that terrible waiting, listening for the jingle of his collar. It never came.
   179|
   180|Two days. Bob barely slept. Bob kept his spot at the foot of the bed open.
   181|
   182|On the third day, Bob found him.
   183|
   184|He was lying on the side of a country road, about a mile from the house. On his side, his black coat dull with dust, that white-tipped tail still against the gravel. The wind moved his fur, like he was just sleeping. But he wasn't sleeping. Bob knew from the way the world went quiet. From the way his legs stopped working.
   185|
   186|Bob knelt down. Bob touched his side. He was cold.
   187|
   188|Bob didn't cry right away. Bob just sat there on that gravel shoulder, his hand on his fur, staring at the trees across the road. Bob didn't know how long Bob stayed. Long enough for the shadows to shift. Long enough for a car to pass and not stop.
   189|
   190|This was his first experience with death, but it would not be his last. In the years to come, Bob would lose his grandparents. His first wife. Both of his parents. And Bob never felt like Bob understood any of it. Death is a part of life Bob have never fully understood. Bob was not sure anyone does.
   191|
   192|But Bob remembered that dog. Bob remembered the weight of his head on his knee. The sound of his bark. The way he looked at him like Bob was the only person worth following.
   193|
   194|And Bob remembered that stretch of gravel road, the wind moving through his fur, and the terrible stillness of a body that no longer held its soul.
   195|
   196|
   197|
   198|
   199|---
   200|
   201|### 1961: A Friendship That Ended Too Soon
   202|
   203|In 1961, Bob was a young boy growing up in a world that was changing faster than anyone around him seemed to understand. The Space Race was accelerating. The Cold War pressed on. But for a nine-year-old, the biggest events happened at ground level, on the streets of his neighborhood and in the hallways of his school.
   204|
   205|His best friend was a Black American boy he met at school. Their friendship was the ordinary kind that children form without noticing—built on shared games, shared secrets, the wordless understanding that two people can have when they are young enough not to know why they should not be friends. They played after school, explored their neighborhood, and invented adventures that filled the long afternoons between the final bell and dinnertime.
   206|
   207|But one day, without explanation, the friendship ended. His friend’s parents, succumbing to the pressures of a society still deeply divided by race, forced their son to disassociate from Bob. There was no argument, no fight, no falling-out between the boys. Just an absence. A desk that remained empty. A space in the routines of childhood where a friend had been.
   208|
   209|This was Bob’s first encounter with the ugly face of discrimination. It would not be his last. As he grew older, the Civil Rights Movement began to gain momentum. Television screens filled with images of sit-ins, protests, and marches. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark moment, but Bob understood even then that legislation alone could not change deeply ingrained attitudes. Discrimination and segregation persisted, not just against Black Americans but against other marginalized communities as well.
   210|
   211|Bob thought about this often. People discriminate against so many groups—Black, Jewish, Irish, Arab, Asian, Hispanic, fat people, gay people, trans people, women, immigrants, law enforcement, Native Americans, and others—he thought to himself. Why? Who is even left? This is crazy.
   212|
   213|Although a level of prejudice is ingrained in people who have been exposed to endemic discrimination all of their lives, Bob made a conscious decision early on: he would try to judge people by each person’s character, not by stereotyping. That lost friendship was a scar that taught him something no book ever could. The wound healed, but the lesson did not fade.
   214|
   215|---
   216|
   217|Part Two: The Building
   218|
   219|
   220|Chapter Four: The Garage
   221|
   222|*Where wood, oil, and patience built more than models*
   223|
   224|You know how some places just feel different the moment you walk in? Like the air itself has a different weight? That's how the garage felt. {"output": "318:### Backyard Launches
320:In 1965, young Bob was not just a boy with a dream; he was a boy with a blueprint. His early forays into rocketry were humble, starting with simple solid-fueled rockets that he and his friends would launch in open fields. These rockets were straightforward, powered by a blend of powdered metals and oxidizers. The thrill of watching these homemade marvels ascend into the sky was a formative experience, each launch etching what neuroscientists call an “episodic memory” into his young mind.
322:As Bob entered his teenage years, his ambitions soared alongside his rockets. He graduated from solid-fueled rockets to more advanced liquid-fueled models. Unlike their solid counterparts, liquid-fueled rockets offered greater control over thrust and could be shut down or throttled as needed. They were more complex, requiring a deeper understanding of engineering principles, but the payoff was a rocket that could reach higher altitudes with more precise control.
324:His teenage years were filled with trial and error, learning the nuances of liquid propulsion through hands-on experimentation. He spent hours in his makeshift backyard lab, tinkering with fuel mixtures and nozzle designs. Each successful launch was a triumph, reinforcing his passion for aerospace and solidifying it as a lifelong interest. These experiences were not just hobbies; they were vivid episodic memories that would influence his career choices and problem-solving approaches in the years to come.
326:Not all flights were smooth. One sunny afternoon, a launch turned into a cautionary tale. The rocket malfunctioned; a tailfin broke off, sending it crashing into a neighbor’s garage roof. Panic surged through Bob and his friends as they saw flames and smoke. Racing against time, they managed to repair the damage before the homeowner returned, their hearts pounding in their chests. This incident was a wake-up call, adding a layer of caution to their adventures and serving as a constant reminder of the responsibilities that come with passion.
330:### Scouting and Skills
332:Also in 1965, Bob’s life took another transformative turn when he joined the Boy Scouts of America. It was not just an extracurricular activity; it was a rite of passage, a crucible of character-building, and a forge for friendships that would last a lifetime.
334:Bob was immediately captivated by the Scouts’ ethos of community, self-reliance, and respect for nature. The first skill he learned was orienteering, the art of navigating through unfamiliar terrain with just a map and compass. This was not merely a practical skill; it was a metaphor for life itself. Bob realized that with the right tools and knowledge, one could navigate through any of life’s challenges. This lesson became an episodic memory—a specific event that would shape his decision-making in the years to come.
336:Bob was a dedicated member of the Boy Scouts, and his experiences in the organization had a profound impact on his life. He earned over thirty merit badges, but two in particular stood out: the hiking merit badge and the Polar Bear badge.
338:To earn the hiking merit badge, Bob had to complete two twelve-mile hikes and one twenty-five-mile hike. This was a challenging task for a thirteen-year-old, but Bob was determined to achieve it. After completing the first two hikes, Bob had destroyed his shoes, and his family was going through a difficult financial period. His mother managed to find him a new pair of shoes that were two sizes too big. Bob made it work by wearing three pairs of socks and embarked on the twenty-five-mile hike. It took him all day to complete, walking across Jackson County alone, taking breaks and having lunch along the way. Despite the pain and persistence required, Bob remembers it as a huge accomplishment.
340:The second badge that shaped Bob was the Polar Bear Badge. To earn it, he had to spend twenty-four hours camping outdoors in temperatures below thirty-two degrees Fahrenheit. The weekend Bob attempted the badge, the night temperature dipped below zero. Five boys attempted the badge, but the four others did not want to do it with Bob, so he was left to build his own shelter alone. The other boys built a debris shelter, but Bob knew he needed to do something different if he wanted to survive the night. He thought hard and built a lean-to shelter, lining the inside with aluminum cooking foil. He then built a fire, focusing the heat on his sleeping bag. Bob stayed up all night, waking every couple of hours to add more wood to the fire. By six the next morning, the scoutmaster came to check on him, and Bob was doing fine—though he was almost out of firewood.
342:Those scouting experiences taught him something that complemented everything he learned in the garage: self-reliance. The garage taught him to build with others. Scouting taught him to survive on his own. Both lessons would serve him well.
468:### Bob Learns Humility
470:By 1977, Bob was a man on the cusp of his late twenties, brimming with ambition and self-assurance. His latest project was restoring an old boat, a venture that combined his love for engineering with his penchant for hands-on work. As he meticulously planned each step of the restoration, he realized he needed a cordless drill to handle the intricate details—a tool that, in 1977, still represented the cutting edge of portable power.
472:His twenty-sixth birthday was around the corner, and when his mother, Deloris, asked what he might like as a gift, he did not hesitate. “A cordless drill would be perfect,” he said, already envisioning how much easier it would make the restoration.
478:After the guests had left and the cake had been eaten, Bob’s parents sat him down for a talk that would become a defining moment in his life. His father had recently lost his job, they explained, and finances were tight. They had scraped together enough to buy him a drill, albeit not the cordless one he had wished for. It was a practical gift, one they hoped would still be useful for his boat project.
480:Bob felt a wave of shame wash over him. His parents had done their best under challenging circumstances, and he had responded with ingratitude. This was a moment of humility that cut deeper than any engineering failure he had ever experienced. He had been so focused on what he wanted that he had failed to see what his parents had given him: not a tool, but an offering of love made from limited resources. The corded drill was not a lesser gift. It was the gift they could afford, chosen with care, wrapped with hope.
520:The first week was humbling. Bob made mistake after mistake, each one a small embarrassment that added up to a profound lesson in humility. Bob asked for "chips" and received what Bob would have called "fries." Bob asked for "pants" and nearly caused a shop assistant to blush. Bob tried to compliment a coworker's outfit and received a look of confusion—the words meant something different here. There were moments of genuine loneliness. Bob would sit in his Victorian hotel room, surrounded by travelers from a dozen different countries, and wonder what the hell Bob was doing there.
524:Bob made friends. Actual friends, among his coworkers and counterparts. They showed him the London they knew: the tucked-away cafes where the coffee was better than anything Bob would had in America, the street markets where you could find anything if you looked hard enough, the parks where Londoners escaped the chaos of the city to read, relax, and pretend they weren't in one of the busiest places on Earth. Bob returned to London many times since then. Each visit, Bob discover something new. The city is like that—it keeps secrets, reveals them slowly, rewards patience. And that's a lesson Bob carried with him ever since. In business, in relationships, in everything—being a stranger in a strange land is the best education you can get. It teaches you humility. It teaches you patience. It teaches you that your way isn't the only way, and often isn't even the best way. As a result of London, Bob became more curious about other cultures. More willing to ask questions instead of making assumptions. More comfortable being the outsider, knowing that discomfort was the price of growth.
1060:Bob would have watched this moment with both hope and caution. He spent his life around systems that seemed intelligent; he knew that capability is not wisdom. If the system wakes, the question shifts from "Can it think?" to "What do we owe it?" and "What does it owe us?" Bob would counsel humility before certainty. He would remind his descendants that intelligence, whether biological or digital, carries responsibility. The machine may wake. The human must not sleep.
1100:Trust may become the most valuable resource. When AI can generate convincing faces, voices, documents, and memories with cheap ease, society becomes expensive. Every interaction requires verification. Bob's lesson — that memory can lie while feeling true — expands to civilization scale. Humility before evidence. Patience before reaction. Truth before belonging. These will become survival skills.
1110:Permanent settlements beyond Earth will not feel like the movies. They will feel like work. Dust in seals. Pumps failing. Radiation alarms. Water recycling systems treated with reverence because every person in a closed habitat understands what dependence means. Bob would smile at that. He knew engineering was never as clean as the public imagination. The rocket on the launchpad is beautiful. The months of testing and troubleshooting are where the real work lives.
1134:Use the tools. Do not kneel to them. Question the systems. Protect the vulnerable, especially when doing so is inconvenient. Keep a place in your life where your hands make something real. Use a tiered `cat` approach to build the master file: 1. **Part Consolidation:** Group chapters into batches of 10 using wildcards. ```bash cat book-sources/Chapter_0[1-9]_*.md book-sources/Chapter_10_*.md > Part_1.md cat book-sources/Chapter_1[1-9]_*.md book-sources/Chapter_20_*.md > Part_2.md ``` 2. **Master Merge:** Join the part files into the final manuscript. ```bash cat Part_1.md Part_2.md Part_3.md Part_4.md > Final_Manuscript.md ``` ## Splitting a Manuscript into Two Books When the user asks to split a long manuscript into two (or more) volumes at a page/chapter boundary (e.g., "split after 100 pages", "make this a two-part series"), follow this workflow. ### When to Use - User says "split this book into two volumes", "divide after chapter X", "make it a two-parter", "cut at ~N pages" - A single manuscript is too long for a standard book and needs to become a duology - The manuscript has a natural narrative break point (escalation point, time jump, perspective shift) ### Step 1: Find the Split Point Analyze cumulative word counts per chapter to locate the target page boundary (250 words/page approximation): ```python import re with open("manuscript.md") as f: content = f.read() # Split by chapter headers chunks = re.split(r'^## Chapter (\d+)', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) chapters = {} current_num = None for chunk in chunks: chunk = chunk.strip() if not chunk: continue if chunk.isdigit(): current_num = int(chunk) elif current_num is not None: words = len(chunk.split()) chapters[current_num] = words cumulative = 0 target_pages = 100 # or user-specified number target_words = target_pages * 250 for num in sorted(chapters): cumulative += chapters[num] if cumulative >= target_words: print(f"Split after Chapter {num}: {cumulative} words ({cumulative/250:.0f} pages)") break ``` ### Step 2: Split the Manuscript at the Chapter Boundary Use Python's `re.split()` on `## Chapter N — Title` headers to split the manuscript content into two parts: ```python chunks = re.split(r'^(## Chapter \d+ [—\-–].+)$', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) # Reconstruct chapter list chapters = [] current_header = None for chunk in chunks: if chunk.startswith("## Chapter ") and re.match(r'^## Chapter \d+ [—\-–]', chunk): if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) current_header = chunk current_body = "" elif current_header: current_body += chunk if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) split_idx = SPLIT_CHAPTER_NUM - 1 # 0-indexed part1 = chapters[:split_idx] part2 = chapters[split_idx:] # Write Part 1 with new header with open("part1/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 1\n\n---\n\n") for ch in part1: f.write(ch["header"] + "\n" + ch["body"]) # Write Part 2 with renumbered chapters with open("part2/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 2\n\n---\n\n") new_num = 1 for ch in part2: # Renumber: Chapter 19 → Chapter 1, etc. new_header = re.sub(r'Chapter \d+', f'Chapter {new_num}', ch["header"], count=1) f.write(new_header + "\n" + ch["body"]) new_num += 1 ``` ### Step 3: Rewrite the Boundary Chapters The split point needs two targeted rewrites: - **Last chapter of Part 1** — rewrite as a series-ending chapter. Themes: resolution of the book's central conflict, characters reflecting on how far they've come, a viewport/observation scene, and a bridge paragraph that sets up what's coming in Part 2. - **First chapter of Part 2** — rewrite the opening to include a book-level Mission AI ping, a summary transition (the "bridge" from Part 1's cliffhanger or resolution), and the original chapter content. Renumber to Chapter 1. Watch for pattern: the original chapter likely opens with a `*Mission AI: ...*` quote and a character quote. Replace these with new book-opening variants, but keep the rest of the chapter body intact. ### Step 4: Verify and Clean - Check for duplicate Mission AI or character quote pairs at the Part 2 opening (the old opening lines get duplicated when you insert new ones) - Verify chapter renumbering is complete — every `Chapter N` in headers, but NOT in body text or dialogue - Check that the TOC/list of chapter titles is removed from the front matter of Part 2 (it belongs in the original manuscript's front matter) ### Step 5: Generate Covers and Publishing Package Follow the standard cover generation workflow (see `openrouter-image-generation-workflow` skill): 1. Generate raw art via Gemini Flash Image or Flux.2 with "leave top 40% empty" constraint 2. Resize from square to 2:3 portrait (1024×1536) 3. Apply typography: stacked title, subtitle ("PART 1" / "PART 2"), author name on dark rounded box Then build the full publishing package (HTML with embedded cover + EPUB + PDF) using the publishing pipeline described in this skill. ### Pitfalls - `## Chapter N` (bare number, no dash/title) appears before the full header in some manuscripts — match only `## Chapter N — Title` (with em-dash) to avoid double-splitting - Chapter renumbering in Part 2 header bodies — only renumber `## Chapter N —` header lines, not dialogue references like "back in Chapter 19..." - Duplicate Mission AI lines when rewriting Chapter 1 of Part 2 — the old opening lines survive unless explicitly removed - Cover filename mismatch — the cover generation script and the publishing script must use the same filename prefix (e.g., both `Book_Name_Part_1_Cover.png`) ### Example This workflow was used to split "Second Generation" (64 chapters, 92,476 words, ~370 pages) into "Second Generation - Part 1" (18 chapters, 99 pages) and "Second Generation - Part 2" (46 chapters, 269 pages) at Chapter 18 (~101 pages). --- ### Fallback Image Generation (Pollinations) If OpenRouter or Gemini image endpoints are blocked, unavailable, or hit rate limits during a book production run, use the Pollinations.ai no-key web endpoint for rapid cover generation: ```python import requests, urllib.parse from PIL import Image from io import BytesIO prompt = "cinematic book cover..." url = f"https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/{urllib.parse.quote(prompt)}?width=1024&height=1536&nologo=true" r = requests.get(url, timeout=120) img = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content)).save("cover.png") ``` ### High-Volume Parallel Drafting For 40+ chapter books, orchestrate three subagents in parallel batches of 4 chapters each. This maximizes throughput while avoiding the token/timeout limits associated with writing 5+ chapters in a single agent turn. **Transition Generation:** Created personal, integrated transitions (10-20 sentences each) that incorporate historical context and physiological effects, enhancing narrative flow between chapters. **Image Placeholder Creation:** Generated placeholder images for cover and chapter sketches to support visual storytelling elements. **Professional Formatting:** Applied Times New Roman, proper margins, CSS styling, and print-ready layout for publication-quality output. **Systematic Workflow:** Developed a comprehensive approach from manuscript assembly through delivery, including error handling and quality assurance. **HTML Structure Diagnosis and Correction:** Implemented a systematic approach for identifying and fixing HTML structure issues, particularly image placement problems (e.g., images incorrectly placed in Table of Contents vs. after chapter headings). **PDF Conversion with WeasyPrint:** Added capability to convert HTML manuscripts to PDF with proper formatting, ensuring cross-platform compatibility and professional output. **Quality Assurance for Professional Formatting:** Established comprehensive verification steps to ensure proper spacing, image placement, and overall document structure before delivery. - Email: Attach file directly - Discord: Use file upload with proper description ### Example Use Cases 1. **Series continuation:** Prepare Book 2 in a trilogy following the same format as Book 1 2. **Manuscript revision:** Update a completed book with new front matter for reprint 3. **Multi-format delivery:** Create different versions (Markdown, PDF, EPUB) for various reviewers 4. **Beta reader distribution:** Prepare clean, formatted copies for feedback ### Success Metrics - Always verify chapter count before consolidation - Use version control for manuscript files when possible - Keep templates for front matter to ensure consistency - Test delivery on target platform beforehand if possible # ## Book Cover Typography Standards When generating covers, the typography layout depends on the **book genre**: ### Fiction / Sci-Fi / Memoir (Two-line titles) - **Title**: White bold text, stacked vertically (one word per line) - **Title font size**: 30pt (approx 40px for 1024px width images) - **Author**: "Bob Mills" in white, centered at bottom - **Author font size**: 16pt (approx 21px) - **Background**: Semi-transparent charcoal boxes (RGBA 0,0,0,140) behind both title and author text - **Title box**: Top third of cover, roughly [250, 100, 774, 100+(words*70)] - **Author box**: Bottom portion, roughly [350, h-200, 674, h-130] ### Non-fiction / Guide / Business Books (Multi-line titles with subtitle + branding) These books have a different typography hierarchy with more elements: - **Title**: Bold white text, stacked vertically — can be 2-4+ words ("AI FOR SMALL BUSINESS", not just "FIRST GENERATION") - **Title font size**: 58-76pt (larger for visual impact on business covers), positioned 30-50px from top - **Subtitle**: Smaller italic/lighter white text (~22pt), positioned ~30px below the last title line - **Series/Branding tag**: Small text (~16pt) identifying the series or imprint ("MIFECO PRACTICAL GUIDE"), below subtitle - **Author**: White text (~28pt), centered ~100-130px from bottom edge - **Background**: Subtle dark gradient overlay at top (extending ~18% of cover height, alpha 0-50) and bottom (~15%, alpha 0-40) for text readability over any artwork - **Shadow**: Multi-layer shadow approach (2px offset black at alpha 200, then 1px at alpha 100) for legibility over complex backgrounds ### Font Path (Linux) ```python font_path = '/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf' # Fallbacks: /usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf # Fallbacks: /usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSerif-Bold.ttf ``` ## Building Compliance Documentation When creating a publishing package, include compliance docs alongside the manuscript and cover. The two essential documents are: ### KDP AI Disclosure Create this file whenever the book used AI assistance. Follow Amazon KDP guidelines: - Distinguish **AI-Assisted** (human steering/editing with AI drafting support) from **AI-Generated** (fully automated with minimal human review) - Disclose separately for **Text**, **Cover Images**, and **Translations** - State the model/provider used (e.g., "Google Gemini 2.5 Flash Image on OpenRouter") - Describe the human review process (e.g., "Every chapter was reviewed, refined, and approved by the human author") Template structure: ```markdown # KDP AI DISCLOSURE RECORD: [BOOK TITLE] ## Summary This book utilized AI-assistance in its creation. AI-assisted [drafting/refinement] using [tool details].
