{"success": true, "name": "openrouter-image-generation-workflow", "description": "Comprehensive workflow for generating images via OpenRouter API with Gemini Flash Image and Flux.2 models, including background processing, error handling, canvas manipulation, typography overlay, vision QA, and HTML integration", "tags": ["image_gen", "openrouter", "workflow", "flux", "background-processing"], "related_skills": ["openrouter-image-generation"], "content": "--- name: openrouter-image-generation-workflow description: Comprehensive workflow for generating images via OpenRouter API with Gemini Flash Image and Flux.2 models, including background processing, error handling, canvas manipulation, typography overlay, vision QA, and HTML integration version: 1.3.0 author: Hermes Agent license: MIT metadata: hermes: tags: [image_gen, openrouter, workflow, flux, background-processing] related_skills: [openrouter-image-generation] --- # OpenRouter Image Generation Workflow This skill documents the complete approach for generating images via OpenRouter API with Flux.2 model, including background processing, error handling, and HTML integration. ## When to Use This Workflow Use this workflow when you need to generate images via OpenRouter API and integrate them into documents. This approach is particularly valuable for: - Generating **individual or series/trilogy book covers** with consistent typography - Chapter header illustrations for manuscripts - Batch image generation with progress tracking - Robust error handling and recovery - HTML document integration **Series/trilogy trigger:** When the user asks to "redo covers" or "regenerate covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., "redo the covers for books 1, 2, and 3"), load this skill and follow the Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline section below. ## Key Components ### 1. Background Processing ```python # Run the script in the background to avoid blocking terminal(background=True, command="python /path/to/script.py > /tmp/log.txt 2>&1 &", notify_on_complete=True) ``` ### 2. API Request Functions #### Flux.2 (standard pattern) ```python def generate_image(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate a single image and save to file. Handles API errors, timeouts, and file verification. """ url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'} payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are an AI assistant that generates images."}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Generate an image:\\n\\n{prompt}\\n\\nReturn as base64 PNG."} ], "modalities": ["image"] } try: response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=120) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() # Extract image data choices = result.get('choices', []) if not choices or 'message' not in choices[0]: raise ValueError("Invalid response structure") images = choices[0]['message'].get('images', []) if not images: raise ValueError("No images in response") img_data = images[0] if not isinstance(img_data, dict) or 'image_url' not in img_data: raise ValueError("Invalid image data") img_url = img_data['image_url'] if not isinstance(img_url, dict) or 'url' not in img_url: raise ValueError("No image URL provided") img_url_str = img_url['url'] if not img_url_str.startswith('data:image/png;base64,'): raise ValueError("Unexpected image format") # Decode and save img_b64 = img_url_str.split(',')[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(img_b64) with open(output_path, 'wb') as f: f.write(img_bytes) # Verify file exists if not Path(output_path).exists(): raise FileNotFoundError("Failed to save image file") return output_path except Exception as e: # Log error and return None for retry print(f"Error generating image: {e}") return None #### Gemini Flash Image (multimodal content format) Use this model (`google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`) via OpenRouter when you need higher-quality, photorealistic cover art. The payload format differs from Flux — it uses a structured content array rather than a plain string: ```python def generate_image_gemini(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image"): """Generate image using Gemini Flash Image via OpenRouter.""" url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "HTTP-Referer": "https://hermes.local", "X-Title": "Hermes Image Generation" } payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt} ] } ] } response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=180) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() images = result["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", []) img_data = images[0] img_url = img_data["image_url"]["url"] if img_url.startswith("data:image/png;base64,"): b64 = img_url.split(",", 1)[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64) elif img_url.startswith("http"): img_resp = requests.get(img_url, timeout=60) img_bytes = img_resp.content with open(output_path, "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) return output_path ``` **Fallback strategy:** Try Gemini first for cover art (better composition and lighting). If it fails, fall back to Flux.2-max and retry as described in batch processing below. **Pitfalls:** - Gemini Flash Image only accepts the `content: [{type: "text", text: "..."}]` format — NOT the string-based content or `modalities` field that Flux uses. - Setting `modalities: ["image"]` on Gemini calls causes a 400 error. - Gemini may return square (1024×1024) images instead of portrait. Be prepared to extend the canvas (see Letterbox technique in Section 7). ### 3. Batch Processing with Progress Tracking ```python def generate_images_batch(prompts, output_dir, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate multiple images with progress tracking and error recovery. Runs in background with notifications on completion. """ success_count = 0 fail_count = 0 failures = [] for name, prompt in prompts.items(): output_path = Path(output_dir) / f"{name}.png" # Generate image result = generate_image(prompt, str(output_path), api_key, model) if result: print(f"✅ Generated {name}") success_count += 1 else: print(f"❌ Failed to generate {name}") fail_count += 1 failures.append(name) # Delay to avoid rate limiting time.sleep(3) print(f"\nSummary: {success_count} succeeded, {fail_count} failed") if failures: print(f"Failed: {', '.join(failures)}") return success_count, fail_count, failures ``` ### 4. HTML Integration ```python def insert_images_into_html(html_path, image_dir, mapping): """ Insert generated images into HTML document. mapping: {placeholder_name: image_filename} """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() for placeholder, image_file in mapping.items(): img_path = Path(image_dir) / image_file if not img_path.exists(): print(f"Warning: {image_file} not found") continue # Create img tag img_tag = f'' # Find insertion point using regex patterns if placeholder == 'cover': # Insert after cover-author div in cover section pattern = r'(
.*?)(
.*?
)' match = re.search(pattern, html_content, re.DOTALL) if match: new_content = match.group(1) + match.group(2) + '\n ' + img_tag + '\n
' html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), new_content) print(f"Inserted cover image") elif placeholder.startswith('chapter'): # Insert after chapter heading h3 tag chapter_num = placeholder.replace('chapter', '') heading = None if chapter_num == '1': heading = "The Builder's Blood" elif chapter_num == '2': heading = "The Navy Way" elif chapter_num == '4': heading = "The Garage Stays Open" elif chapter_num == '5': heading = "The TV Repair Shop" elif chapter_num == '6': heading = "The Engineering of Everything" elif chapter_num == '7': heading = "Chapter xx: Engineer vs. Executive" # Fallback else: heading = f"Chapter {chapter_num}" pattern = rf']*>{heading}' match = re.search(pattern, html_content) if match: new_content = html_content.replace( match.group(0), match.group(0) + '\n' + img_tag + '\n' ) html_content = new_content print(f"Inserted chapter {chapter_num} image") # Write modified HTML with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) # Remove duplicate images if any cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path) ``` ### 5. Duplicate Cleanup ```python def cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path): """ Remove duplicate image tags that may have been inserted multiple times. """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() # Find all cover image tags cover_img_pattern = r'' matches = list(re.finditer(cover_img_pattern, html_content)) if len(matches) > 1: # Keep only the first one after cover div cover_div_end = html_content.find('', html_content.find('
')) if cover_div_end != -1: # Find first cover img after cover div first_valid_img = None for match in matches: if match.start() > cover_div_end: first_valid_img = match break if first_valid_img: # Remove all others for match in matches: if match != first_valid_img: html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), '') print(f"Removed {len(matches)-1} duplicate cover images") # Write back with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) ``` ## Lessons Learned from Trial and Error ### 1. API Response Structure - The image URL is deeply nested in the JSON response - Need to handle cases where fields might be missing - Base64 data URL requires stripping the prefix before decoding ### 2. Error Handling - API calls can fail for many reasons (network, rate limiting, model issues) - Always verify files are created successfully - Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures - Log errors with context for debugging ### 3. HTML Integration - Understanding the HTML structure is crucial for correct image placement - Use regex patterns that are specific enough but flexible - Handle cases where insertion points might not exist - Clean up duplicates from multiple insertion attempts - For files sent over Telegram or similar channels, prefer embedding the generated cover as a base64 `data:` URI so the HTML stays self-contained ### 4. Performance Considerations - Running in background prevents timeouts from blocking - Include delays between requests to avoid rate limiting - Verify file existence before proceeding - Use efficient string operations for HTML manipulation ### 5. Robustness - Always check if files exist before trying to read them - Handle different image formats gracefully - Provide meaningful error messages - Clean up temporary files if needed - If local config files are malformed YAML, extract the needed API key with a targeted regex instead of assuming the whole config can be parsed safely - **Sourcing API keys from .env:** When running in terminal sessions or cron jobs, environment variables from the agent's session may not propagate. Read the key directly from `~/.hermes/.env` as a fallback: ```python env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")) api_key = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") if not api_key and env_file.exists(): for line in open(env_file): if line.startswith("OPENROUTER_API_KEY=") and "***" not in line: api_key = line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip("'\"") ``` ### 6. Cover-Generation QA Loop - For premium cover art, one generation is often not enough - After generating a candidate, run vision QA to assess: negative space for title/author, absence of baked-in gibberish text, clutter level, and whether the image reads as a real cover instead of generic concept art - If the image is too busy, regenerate with stricter prompt constraints such as: `leave generous negative space`, `no logos/text/symbols`, `avoid clutter`, and `main subject in middle band` - This iterative generate → critique → regenerate loop produces materially better book-cover results than accepting the first image ### 6.5 Pre-Typography Canvas Adjustment (Generate → QA → Extend → Text) Do NOT blindly regenerate when the raw image has good art but poor composition. Instead, use a **two-pass QA approach**: **Pass 1 — Assess the raw image:** 1. Generate the raw image (no text, no overlays) 2. Run vision QA asking specifically about: - Does the top 40% have enough clean negative space for stacked title text? - Does the bottom 15% have clean space for the author name? - What's the actual image size and aspect ratio? (Gemini often returns 1024×1024 squares) - Is the subject positioned too high/low/off-center for a book cover layout? 3. Based on QA feedback, decide: regenerate with a better prompt OR extend the canvas **Canvas extension (preferred when art quality is good but composition is off):** - If the Earth/planet is too high → add 60% of extra height to the top, 40% to bottom - If the subject is centered but the image is square → extend both top AND bottom evenly - If the subject is too low → add more to the bottom, less to the top - **Never extend less than 200px at top** — the title zone needs at least 200-300px of pure black for a 2-5 word stacked title at 52-58pt - Always resize to **1024×1536 (2:3)** — standard book cover ratio **Pass 2 — Add typography onto the adjusted canvas:** - Once the canvas has clean black letterbox zones, add typography on top - Text on pure black needs only a 1px shadow, NO background boxes - Run a second vision QA to verify text placement ### 7. Cover Typography and Branding (Final Polish) When generating retail-ready book covers, follow these specific design standards for professional consistency: - **Typography Specifications:** Users often require specific typography (e.g., "30pt white title, one word per line, stacked"). For 1024x1536 covers, "30pt" typically translates to approximately 40 pixels in height, and "16pt" translates to 21-22 pixels. - **Transparency for Visibility:** To ensure background art is not "occluded" (blocked), use semi-transparent black boxes (e.g., `fill=(0,0,0,120)` in PIL) rather than solid black bars. - **Vertical Title Stacking:** For long titles or specific aesthetic requirements, stack words vertically (one word per line). This maximizes the "action zone" of the background art and prevent cutoff. - **Even Spacing Calculation:** Calculate line heights and start position mathematically to center the stacked text vertically within the title zone: ```python line_h = int(title_font_size * 1.2) # consistent inter-word spacing total_title_h = line_h * len(title_words) # total height of stacked title title_zone_h = int(target_h * 0.35) # title occupies top 35% of canvas title_start_y = (title_zone_h - total_title_h) // 2 # center within zone ``` This ensures mathematically equal spacing between every word, avoiding the "cramped at top, loose at bottom" look of hardcoded offsets. - **Author Placement:** Center the author name horizontally at the bottom of the cover (e.g., `h - 160` for a 1536px height). - **Canvas Extension (Letterbox Technique):** When the AI-generated image lacks enough negative space at the top (e.g., Earth/planet is too high), add pure black bars by extending the canvas rather than re-generating: ```python from PIL import Image target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 # 2:3 book cover ratio img = Image.open(input_path) orig_w, orig_h = img.size ratio = target_w / orig_w img_resized = img.resize((target_w, int(orig_h * ratio)), Image.LANCZOS) extra_h = target_h - img_resized.size[1] top_extend = int(extra_h * 0.6) # 60% to top, 40% to bottom bottom_extend = extra_h - top_extend canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0)) canvas.paste(img_resized, (0, top_extend)) ``` This creates clean black letterbox zones for the title (top) and author (bottom) with zero risk of text overlapping artwork. - **Full-Bleed Crop (alternative to letterbox):** When the AI image is square (1024×1024) and the center has valuable art, scale it up to fill the portrait height and crop the sides instead of adding black bars. This eliminates white sidebars and gives a professional full-bleed look: ```python target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 img = Image.open(input_path) scale_h = target_h / img.size[1] # e.g. 1536/1024 = 1.5 img_scaled = img.resize((int(img.size[0] * scale_h), target_h), Image.LANCZOS) x_offset = (img_scaled.size[0] - target_w) // 2 # center-crop width canvas = img_scaled.crop((x_offset, 0, x_offset + target_w, target_h)) ``` **When to use which:** Letterbox (black bars) when the art has important content at the very edges that shouldn't be cropped. Full-bleed crop when the art is centered and the edges are uniform (sky, ground, space) — this looks more professional and avoids the "boxed-in" appearance. - **Gradient Overlay for Busy Backgrounds:** When the artwork has bright elements that reduce text legibility (e.g., a glowing cave opening, a lit planet, a bright horizon), use a subtle dark gradient at the top and/or bottom of the image rather than solid black bars or opaque boxes: ```python overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0)) draw = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay) # Top gradient (progressive dark fade) grad_height = int(target_h * 0.28) # fade from ~0 to 28% of cover height for y in range(grad_height): alpha = int(100 * (1 - y / grad_height)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 70))) # Bottom gradient (for author name readability) bot_grad = int(target_h * 0.10) # bottom 10% for y in range(bot_grad): alpha = int(80 * (y / bot_grad)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, target_h - bot_grad + y, target_w, target_h - bot_grad + y + 1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 60))) ``` This preserves the artwork underneath while ensuring text remains readable. Works best in combination with a subtle 2px text shadow. - **Inch-Based and Percentage Font Adjustments:** After initial QA, users often request specific positioning or sizing tweaks. Handle these with math: - **"1.5 inches from the top":** At standard book cover resolution (1024×1536 ≈ 170-200 DPI for a 6×9 book), 1.5 inches ≈ 255-300 pixels. Calculate: `margin_px = int(1.5 * (target_h / 9))` where 9 is the cover height in inches. ```python # For a 6×9 cover at 1024×1536: dpi = target_h / 9 # ~170 DPI title_top_margin = int(1.5 * dpi) # ~256px from top edge ``` - **"Increase font size by X%":** Multiply the current size and round to nearest integer: `new_size = int(old_size * 1.30)` for a 30% increase. Apply to both title and author font sizes consistently. - **Multi-round iteration pattern:** When the user gives successive positioning/sizing feedback, keep a single Python script and patch individual parameters (title_start_y, font_size, top_extend_ratio) rather than rewriting from scratch. Re-run only the affected book after each change. - **Per-book canvas ratios:** Different books in a series may need different top extension ratios (0.60-0.75). Document the per-book ratio in a dict alongside the font specs so the typography script stays DRY. - **Text Rendering with Shadow:** For pure black letterbox zones, no background box is needed — just drop a subtle 1px shadow for polish. When text must sit on the art itself, use semi-transparent boxes instead. - **Post-Typography Vision QA:** After overlaying text, run a second vision QA pass specifically asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Equivalent font sizes for title vs author - Margin bleed safety (stay 5-10% from edges) If QA flags issues, correct the script and re-run before declaring the cover done. #### Selection rule of thumb For sci-fi covers, prefer the candidate with: 1. strongest title-space contrast, 2. clearest sense of scale/civilization, 3. no embedded text/watermarks, 4. recognizable transportation corridors/roads, 5. minimal visual clutter in the title zone. ## Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline When the user asks to "redo the covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., a 3-book trilogy), follow this end-to-end pipeline to produce N coordinated covers with consistent typography and then hand off to the publishing package builder. ### Pipeline Steps **Step 1 — Plan the series prompts** Write one prompt per book. Each prompt must share a consistent structure: - Same aspect ratio requirement (2:3 portrait, 1024×1536) - Same negative space constraints (top 40% clean for title, bottom 15% clean for author) - Same "no text/logos/watermarks" rule - Different subject/scene per book that advances the series visually Example (sci-fi trilogy): ``` Book 1 (First Generation): Mars canyon city — domes in a deep canyon, red dusty landscape Book 2 (Second Generation): Lava tube habitat — underground colony, warm glow, mineral walls Book 3 (Third Generation): Alien hive ship — mysterious bioluminescent ship, deep space ``` Run the prompts in a single Python script with `notify_on_complete=True` to batch-generate all N backgrounds in sequence. Include `time.sleep(3)` between generations to avoid rate limits. **Step 2 — QA each raw image** After all backgrounds are generated, run vision_analyze on each one, asking specifically: - Is the top 40% clean enough for stacked white title text? - Is the bottom 15% clean for the author name? - Are there any embedded text, watermarks, or digital artifacts? - Is the aspect ratio suitable (square needs canvas extension)? Note which books need canvas adjustments vs. which are ready. **Step 3 — Apply consistent typography across the series** Write a single Python script that processes all N images. The script must: - Use the SAME font path for all books (DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf or LiberationSans-Bold.ttf) - Use the SAME typography rules (font size may vary by word count, but style is identical) - Use the SAME author name placement - Extend square (1024×1024) images to portrait (1024×1536) with black bars (60-75% top, 25-40% bottom) **Define per-book parameters in a dict** so adjustments are data-driven: ```python books = { "First_Generation": { "title_words": ["FIRST", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 58, "top_extend_ratio": 0.70, # more top room if subject is high }, "Second_Generation": { "title_words": ["SECOND", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 52, "top_extend_ratio": 0.68, "add_top_gradient": True, # if bright elements in title zone }, } ``` This makes it easy to tweak one book without touching the others. Per-book adjustments: - If a book's subject is too high (top 40% cluttered), increase the top extension ratio (e.g., 0.75 instead of 0.60) - If a bright light source sits in the title zone, add a subtle dark gradient overlay (alpha 0-80 over the first 50-100px of art) - Ensure every word of the stacked title ends before the artwork begins — verify mathematically: `word_y + text_height_approx < art_start_y` **Step 4 — QA each final cover** Run vision_analyze on each finished cover asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Any text overlapping the artwork boundary - If any issues are found, fix the script and re-run only that book **Step 5 — Hand off to package builder** Once all N covers pass QA, tell the user the covers are ready and then either: - If this is for an existing package, patch `manuscript-preparation-and-delivery` to rebuild the zip - If this is a new package, build a series/trilogy package structure (see manuscript-preparation-and-delivery skill) ### Common Pitfalls - **Inconsistent prompt structure** — Always include "leave generous negative space at top 40%" in every prompt. The AI will default to centering the subject if you don't. - **Square output from Gemini** — Gemini Flash Image often returns 1024×1024 squares regardless of prompt. Always plan for canvas extension. - **Not checking overlap** — After typography, always verify the last word of the stacked title doesn't overlap the artwork. If it does, increase the top extension ratio. - **Batch failures** — If one book's generation fails, don't restart the whole batch. Just regenerate that one book. ## When This Approach Works Well - **Batch image generation**: Perfect for generating multiple images with different prompts - **HTML integration**: Seamlessly integrates generated images into existing HTML documents - **Error recovery**: Handles failures gracefully and continues processing - **Progress tracking**: Provides clear feedback on success/failure rates ## Limitations - **API dependent**: Requires OpenRouter API access and a valid API key - **Model specific**: Uses Flux.2 model; may need adjustments for other models - **HTML structure dependent**: Requires understanding of target HTML structure - **Rate limits**: Subject to OpenRouter's rate limits ## Best Practices 1. **Test with a single image first** before batch processing 2. **Include proper error handling** for all API interactions 3. **Verify file creation** after each generation 4. **Use appropriate delays** between requests to avoid rate limiting 5. **Clean up duplicates** if running multiple times 6. **Monitor progress** and log errors for debugging ## Related Skills - `openrouter-image-generation` (basic skill) - `html-integration` (for HTML manipulation) - `background-processing` (for running tasks asynchronously) ", "path": "openrouter-image-generation-workflow/SKILL.md", "skill_dir": "/home/bob/.hermes/skills/openrouter-image-generation-workflow", "linked_files": null, "usage_hint": null, "required_environment_variables": [], "required_commands": [], "missing_required_environment_variables": [], "missing_credential_files": [], "missing_required_commands": [], "setup_needed": false, "setup_skipped": false, "readiness_status": "available", "metadata": {"hermes": {"tags": ["image_gen", "openrouter", "workflow", "flux", "background-processing"], "related_skills": ["openrouter-image-generation"]}}}

mid_band = img.crop((0, int(h*0.35), w, int(h*0.65)))

def avg_bright(im):
    p = list(im.getdata())
    return sum((r+g+b)//3 for r,g,b in p) / len(p)

print(f"Top 40% avg brightness: {avg_bright(top_band):.0f}/255")

print(f"Bottom 15% avg brightness: {avg_bright(bot_band):.0f}/255")

target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536

# Scale image to fill height
scale = target_h / h
new_w = int(w * scale)
new_h = target_h
img_scaled = img.resize((new_w, new_h), Image.LANCZOS)

# Center-crop or letterbox depending on content
# For square -> 2:3, we scale up to match height and crop sides
if new_w > target_w:
    # Crop sides
    x_offset = (new_w - target_w) // 2
    canvas = img_scaled.crop((x_offset, 0, x_offset + target_w, target_h))
    method = "crop sides (full bleed)"
else:
    # Letterbox sides (less likely for square->portrait)
    canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0))
    x_offset = (target_w - new_w) // 2
    canvas.paste(img_scaled, (x_offset, 0))
    method = "letterbox sides"

Review the conversation above and update the skill library. Be ACTIVE — most sessions produce at least one skill update, even if small. A pass that does nothing is a missed learning opportunity, not a neutral outcome.

Target shape of the library: CLASS-LEVEL skills, each with a rich SKILL.md and a `references/` directory for session-specific detail. Not a long flat list of narrow one-session-one-skill entries. This shapes HOW you update, not WHETHER you update.

Signals to look for (any one of these warrants action):
  • User corrected your style, tone, format, legibility, or verbosity. Frustration signals like 'stop doing X', 'this is too verbose', 'don't format like this', 'why are you explaining', 'just give me the answer', 'you always do Y and I hate it', or an explicit 'remember this' are FIRST-CLASS skill signals, not just memory signals. Update the relevant skill(s) to embed the preference so the next session starts already knowing.
  • User corrected your workflow, approach, or sequence of steps. Encode the correction as a pitfall or explicit step in the skill that governs that class of task.
  • Non-trivial technique, fix, workaround, debugging path, or tool-usage pattern emerged that a future session would benefit from. Capture it.
  • A skill that got loaded or consulted this session turned out to be wrong, missing a step, or outdated. Patch it NOW.

Preference order — prefer the earliest action that fits, but do pick one when a signal above fired:
  1. UPDATE A CURRENTLY-LOADED SKILL. Look back through the conversation for skills the user loaded via /skill-name or you read via skill_view. If any of them covers the territory of the new learning, PATCH that one first. It is the skill that was in play, so it's the right one to extend.
  2. UPDATE AN EXISTING UMBRELLA (via skills_list + skill_view). If no loaded skill fits but an existing class-level skill does, patch it. Add a subsection, a pitfall, or broaden a trigger.
  3. ADD A SUPPORT FILE under an existing umbrella. Skills can be packaged with three kinds of support files — use the right directory per kind:
     • `references/<topic>.md` — session-specific detail (error transcripts, reproduction recipes, provider quirks) AND condensed knowledge banks: quoted research, API docs, external authoritative excerpts, or domain notes you found while working on the problem. Write it concise and for the value of the task, not as a full mirror of upstream docs.
     • `templates/<name>.<ext>` — starter files meant to be copied and modified (boilerplate configs, scaffolding, a known-good example the agent can `reproduce with modifications`).
     • `scripts/<name>.<ext>` — statically re-runnable actions the skill can invoke directly (verification scripts, fixture generators, deterministic probes, anything the agent should run rather than hand-type each time).
     Add support files via skill_manage action=write_file with file_path starting 'references/', 'templates/', or 'scripts/'. The umbrella's SKILL.md should gain a one-line pointer to any new support file so future agents know it exists.
  4. CREATE A NEW CLASS-LEVEL UMBRELLA SKILL when no existing skill covers the class. The name MUST be at the class level. The name MUST NOT be a specific PR number, error string, feature codename, library-alone name, or 'fix-X / debug-Y / audit-Z-today' session artifact. If the proposed name only makes sense for today's task, it's wrong — fall back to (1), (2), or (3).

User-preference embedding (important): when the user expressed a style/format/workflow preference, the update belongs in the SKILL.md body, not just in memory. Memory captures 'who the user is and what the current situation and state of your operations are'; skills capture 'how to do this class of task for this user'. When they complain about how you handled a task, the skill that governs that task needs to carry the lesson.

If you notice two existing skills that overlap, note it in your reply — the background curator handles consolidation at scale.

'Nothing to save.' is a real option but should NOT be the default. If the session ran smoothly with no corrections and produced no new technique, just say 'Nothing to save.' and stop. Otherwise, act.

User says "split this book into two volumes", "divide after chapter X", "make it a two-parter", "cut at ~N pages" - A single manuscript is too long for a standard book and needs to become a duology - The manuscript has a natural narrative break point (escalation point, time jump, perspective shift) ### Step 1: Find the Split Point Analyze cumulative word counts per chapter to locate the target page boundary (250 words/page approximation): ```python import re with open("manuscript.md") as f: content = f.read() # Split by chapter headers chunks = re.split(r'^## Chapter (\d+)', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) chapters = {} current_num = None for chunk in chunks: chunk = chunk.strip() if not chunk: continue if chunk.isdigit(): current_num = int(chunk) elif current_num is not None: words = len(chunk.split()) chapters[current_num] = words cumulative = 0 target_pages = 100 # or user-specified number target_words = target_pages * 250 for num in sorted(chapters): cumulative += chapters[num] if cumulative >= target_words: print(f"Split after Chapter {num}: {cumulative} words ({cumulative/250:.0f} pages)") break ``` ### Step 2: Split the Manuscript at the Chapter Boundary Use Python's `re.split()` on `## Chapter N — Title` headers to split the manuscript content into two parts: ```python chunks = re.split(r'^(## Chapter \d+ [—\-–].+)$', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) # Reconstruct chapter list chapters = [] current_header = None for chunk in chunks: if chunk.startswith("## Chapter ") and re.match(r'^## Chapter \d+ [—\-–]', chunk): if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) current_header = chunk current_body = "" elif current_header: current_body += chunk if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) split_idx = SPLIT_CHAPTER_NUM - 1 # 0-indexed part1 = chapters[:split_idx] part2 = chapters[split_idx:] # Write Part 1 with new header with open("part1/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 1\n\n---\n\n") for ch in part1: f.write(ch["header"] + "\n" + ch["body"]) # Write Part 2 with renumbered chapters with open("part2/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 2\n\n---\n\n") new_num = 1 for ch in part2: # Renumber: Chapter 19 → Chapter 1, etc. new_header = re.sub(r'Chapter \d+', f'Chapter {new_num}', ch["header"], count=1) f.write(new_header + "\n" + ch["body"]) new_num += 1 ``` ### Step 3: Rewrite the Boundary Chapters The split point needs two targeted rewrites: - **Last chapter of Part 1** — rewrite as a series-ending chapter. Themes: resolution of the book's central conflict, characters reflecting on how far they've come, a viewport/observation scene, and a bridge paragraph that sets up what's coming in Part 2. - **First chapter of Part 2** — rewrite the opening to include a book-level Mission AI ping, a summary transition (the "bridge" from Part 1's cliffhanger or resolution), and the original chapter content. Renumber to Chapter 1. Watch for pattern: the original chapter likely opens with a `*Mission AI: ...*` quote and a character quote. Replace these with new book-opening variants, but keep the rest of the chapter body intact. ### Step 4: Verify and Clean - Check for duplicate Mission AI or character quote pairs at the Part 2 opening (the old opening lines get duplicated when you insert new ones) - Verify chapter renumbering is complete — every `Chapter N` in headers, but NOT in body text or dialogue - Check that the TOC/list of chapter titles is removed from the front matter of Part 2 (it belongs in the original manuscript's front matter) ### Step 5: Generate Covers and Publishing Package Follow the standard cover generation workflow (see `openrouter-image-generation-workflow` skill): 1. Generate raw art via Gemini Flash Image or Flux.2 with "leave top 40% empty" constraint 2. Resize from square to 2:3 portrait (1024×1536) 3. Apply typography: stacked title, subtitle ("PART 1" / "PART 2"), author name on dark rounded box Then build the full publishing package (HTML with embedded cover + EPUB + PDF) using the publishing pipeline described in this skill. ### Pitfalls - `## Chapter N` (bare number, no dash/title) appears before the full header in some manuscripts — match only `## Chapter N — Title` (with em-dash) to avoid double-splitting - Chapter renumbering in Part 2 header bodies — only renumber `## Chapter N —` header lines, not dialogue references like "back in Chapter 19..." - Duplicate Mission AI lines when rewriting Chapter 1 of Part 2 — the old opening lines survive unless explicitly removed - Cover filename mismatch — the cover generation script and the publishing script must use the same filename prefix (e.g., both `Book_Name_Part_1_Cover.png`) ### Example This workflow was used to split "Second Generation" (64 chapters, 92,476 words, ~370 pages) into "Second Generation - Part 1" (18 chapters, 99 pages) and "Second Generation - Part 2" (46 chapters, 269 pages) at Chapter 18 (~101 pages). --- ### Fallback Image Generation (Pollinations) If OpenRouter or Gemini image endpoints are blocked, unavailable, or hit rate limits during a book production run, use the Pollinations.ai no-key web endpoint for rapid cover generation: ```python import requests, urllib.parse from PIL import Image from io import BytesIO prompt = "cinematic book cover..." url = f"https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/{urllib.parse.quote(prompt)}?width=1024&height=1536&nologo=true" r = requests.get(url, timeout=120) img = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content)).save("cover.png") ``` ### High-Volume Parallel Drafting For 40+ chapter books, orchestrate three subagents in parallel batches of 4 chapters each. AI-use record for retailer compliance ``` When auditing memoirs or manuscripts that used AI-assisted writing, check for and remove these templated transition artifacts: ### Common AI Transition Patterns to Remove These patterns indicate placeholder AI-generated transitions, not real content: - `"Leaving behind 'X' and turning toward 'Y', I inhabited a mental landscape..."` - `"As the memory of 'X' gave way to the story of 'Y'..."` - `"Moving from 'X' to 'Y', I inhabited what I've come to think of as..."` - `"The shift from contemplating 'X' to engaging with 'Y' carried me through..."` - `"Between the recollection of 'X' and the unfolding of 'Y', my mind rested in..."` - `"As I moved from reflecting on 'X' to confronting 'Y', I found myself in..."` - `"In that space, I began to see connections I had missed before..."` - `"What I discovered there changed how I understood both experiences..."` - `"creative tension between memory and possibility"` - `"my mind rested in a space of integration"` - `"memories blend with anticipation"` - `"psychological threshold"` ### Third-Person POV Conversion Artifacts (Memoir Specific) When a memoir was written in first-person and later converted to third-person ("I" → "Bob"), these residual artifacts commonly survive conversion and must be caught in editorial review: **"Bob would [verb]" where past tense needed:** This is the most common artifact. The converter replaces "I would" literally instead of simplifying to past tense. - `"Bob would ordered"` → `"Bob had ordered"` (or `"Bob ordered"`) - `"Bob would learned"` → `"Bob had learned"` - `"Bob would said"` → `"Bob had said"` (or `"Bob said"`) - `"Bob would gotten"` → `"Bob had gotten"` - `"Bob would had"` → `"Bob had"` Search: `Bob would (ordered|learned|said|gotten|had|asked|told|made|built|known|gone)` **Verb agreement errors from "I"-to-"Bob" substitution:** The converter replaces "I" with "Bob" without adjusting verb conjugation. - `"Bob carry"` → `"Bob carries"` (also: Bob know → knows, Bob have → has, Bob remember → remembers, Bob wish → wishes, Bob discover → discovers) - `"Bob still carry"` → `"Bob still carries"` **Auxiliary verb + past tense errors:** - `"Did Bob remembered"` → `"Did Bob remember"` (main verb after "did" should be base form) - `"Bob only remember"` → `"Bob only remembers"` (subject-verb agreement) **Double-ed endings:** - `"remembereded"` → `"remembered"` Likely from regex replacement that added "ed" to an already-past-tense verb. **First-person pronoun residue in third-person narrative:** - `"inches from mine"` → `"inches from his"` - `"curved away from mine"` → `"curved away from his"` - `"Everything after is mine"` → `"Everything after is his"` Look for bare `"mine"` at end of possessive phrases. **"Transition: [Title]" sections that appear twice:** When content from two source documents is merged, section header + paragraph pairs sometimes duplicate. Search for exact duplicates of any "Transition:" header line. **Detection script:** ```python import re pov_patterns = { "Bob_would_verb": re.compile(r"Bob would (ordered|learned|said|gotten|had|asked|told|made|built|known|gone)"), "Bob_verb_agreement": re.compile(r"Bob (carry|know|have|remember|wish|discover) s?\\b"), "mine_residue": re.compile(r"(from|of|to) mine\\b"), "remembereded": re.compile(r"remembereded"), "Did_Bob_remembered": re.compile(r"Did Bob remembered"), } for label, pattern in pov_patterns.items(): matches = [(i+1, line.strip()) for i, line in enumerate(lines) if pattern.search(line)] if matches: print(f"POV artifact '{label}': {len(matches)} occurrences") ``` ### Cleaning Workflow 1. Search all lines for the patterns above 2. Remove matching lines and adjacent empty lines 3. Verify zero remaining matches 4. Renumber chapters sequentially 5. Audit Part headers for duplicates or sequence errors 6. Regenerate final HTML/CSS with correct structure ### Code for Pattern Detection ```python import re ai_indicators = [ "gave way to the story of", "I inhabited a mental landscape", "creative tension between memory", "I inhabited what I've come to think of", "my mind rested in a space of integration", "memories blend with anticipation", "psychological threshold", ] for i, line in enumerate(lines): for ind in ai_indicators: if ind in line: ai_lines.append((i, line.strip())) break ``` ## Pollinations Cover Generation: Known Issues and Fixes ### Common Failures 1. **Timeouts (120s+)** — The Pollinations API can be slow.
